title: Things That Help: One Fourth Grade Teacher's Simple Method for Positive Parent Contacts During Distance Learning ontacts-during-distance-learning
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares a workload-conscious classroom management tactic sent in by fourth-grade teacher Marisa Silver: rather than the informal curbside chats she used to have with parents at pickup, she now emails six families a day with a brief note of encouragement about their child, cycling through her whole roster in a week during distance learning. Stuart unpacks why the tactic works so well, highlighting its scalability, its use of a simple tracking system to make sure no student is missed, and its refusal to be derailed by anticipated obstacles like bad email addresses or unresponsive parents. He connects the practice to established research on positive parent contact and teacher credibility, arguing it builds trust cheaply even when so much else about the school year is unpredictable. The post closes by praising Silver's focus on what she can control rather than what she can't — a theme that recurs throughout Stuart's pandemic-era writing.
points: A simple numeric target (six parent-encouragement emails per day) turns a good intention into a sustainable, trackable habit rather than an occasional impulse.
A dedicated roster for tracking positive contacts — separate from grading or documentation — keeps a teacher honest about reaching every student, not just the easy or memorable ones.
Refusing to let anticipated obstacles (bad email addresses, silent parents, nothing nice to say) stall the practice keeps momentum even in an imperfect system.
Small, controllable acts of parent outreach build teacher credibility and trust even when the bigger structural problems of the school year are out of a teacher's hands.
quotes: During distance learning no such opportunity exists for informal chats with parents. So this week I have been emailing 6 families per day (6 x 5 days = 30 kids) with just a quick note of encouragement and telling them that their kid is doing a good job in class.

My hope is that this will lead to higher engagement and trust in me as their kid's teacher this year. I can do little to change the format of how we are teaching or the timeline for when we will return to in-person learning. But I always have a few minutes to spare to write a nice email to a family.

Marisa takes something that we know works well — positive parent contact — and shifts it into the simple, enjoyable practice of writing a brief, electronic note to one parent at a time about something she appreciates in each student.
Too often, we trust ourselves too much — simple methods like clipboard tracking help keep us honest.

She's not waylaid on the imperfections and the “what ifs.” What if someone's email address doesn't work? What if a family doesn't respond? What if I don't have anything positive to say about a particular student right now?
For those parents that the intervention does positively affect — most, I think it's safe to suspect — teacher credibility is now a bit more established in the home.
